--- title: "Partial effects" description: "A partial dependence plot draws how a model's prediction changes along one input, averaged over every station, and ICE curves draw the same change station by station. On the survey they find the temperature hump at nearly every station, and show that the depth curve describes the model, not the species." order: 2 categories: [interpretation] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## Partial effects draw how a prediction changes along one input [Feature importance](feature-importance.qmd) says how much a model relies on an input, but not whether the prediction rises or falls with it, or where it peaks. **Partial effects** draw that shape. [Linearity and nonlinearity](../06-assumptions-limitations/linearity-and-nonlinearity.qmd) drew one: a random forest's prediction across temperature, with the other inputs held at typical values. That is one slice, and held at other values the forest's curve could change shape. This page draws curves that do not depend on that choice, one averaged over every station and one for each station. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## A partial dependence plot averages the curve over every station A **partial dependence plot** starts from the data the model was fitted to. Set one input to the same value in every row, keep every other input as it was recorded, and predict each row. The average of those predictions is one point on the curve. Repeat for each value along the input's range, and the points make the curve. It works for any model, because it only needs predictions. ::: {.diagram} ![Partial dependence in three steps: give every row the same value of one input and keep the others, predict each row and move the value along its range so each row traces a curve, then average the rows' curves.](img/partial-dependence.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. Set one input, every row gets one value: a small table with inputs A, B and C, where every cell of column A reads 40 and the shaded cells of B and C are kept. Predict each row, one ICE curve per row: five orange humped curves of different heights against input A, with a dashed line at 40 marking where each row's prediction was made. Average, the partial dependence: the same five curves in grey with a thick green curve through their middle, their average. A note says that where the rows' curves differ in shape, the average hides it, so look at both."} ::: ## ICE curves show the same sweep station by station Before averaging, each row has its own curve: its prediction as the one input moves and the rest of the row stays put. These are **individual conditional expectation (ICE) curves**, and the partial dependence is their average. If they share one shape and differ only in height, the average describes them well. If they peak in different places or cross, the effect of the input depends on the others, an interaction of the kind [Linearity and nonlinearity](../06-assumptions-limitations/linearity-and-nonlinearity.qmd) showed a forest can learn, and the average alone would hide it. ## A sweep can build stations the survey never had Setting depth to the shallowest value in every row pairs it with every station's recorded temperature, including the cold water of the deepest stations. Few or no such stations exist, so there the model is extrapolating. The curves on this page run only over the middle 90% of each input's values, where most stations lie, and are read where the inputs' combinations look like the data. ## Worked example The random forest of [Linearity and nonlinearity](../06-assumptions-limitations/linearity-and-nonlinearity.qmd), 500 trees on the six inputs of [Regression for counts](../03-supervised-learning/count-regression.qmd), is fitted to the same training sites. Its partial dependence is compared with the one slice, then its ICE curves are drawn, and finally position is added as an input to see whether the depth curve changes. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() inputs <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season") split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) test <- testing(split) forest_on <- function(columns) { forest_recipe <- recipe(reformulate(columns, "abundance"), data = train) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) forest_model <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 123) |> set_mode("regression") workflow(forest_recipe, forest_model) |> fit(train) } forest <- forest_on(inputs) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.inspection import partial_dependence from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) train = survey.iloc[train_rows].reset_index(drop=True) test = survey.iloc[test_rows].reset_index(drop=True) numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] def forest_on(numeric): recipe = ColumnTransformer( [("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False), categorical)]) # max_features and min_samples_leaf match ranger's defaults model = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, max_features="sqrt", min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=123) forest = Pipeline([("recipe", recipe), ("model", model)]) return forest.fit(train[numeric + categorical], train["abundance"]) forest = forest_on(numeric) ``` ::: ::: ### Partial dependence misses the depth peak as the slice did Each input is set in turn to 40 values across the middle 90% of its range, and every training station is predicted at each. The partial dependence is the average at each value; the slice holds the other inputs at typical values (sand, summer, the median of the rest), as Linearity and nonlinearity did. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # every training station's prediction with one input set to each of 40 # values over the middle 90% of its range sweep <- function(fitted, input) { ends <- quantile(train[[input]], c(0.05, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE) map(seq(ends[1], ends[2], length.out = 40), \(level) { swept <- train swept[[input]] <- level tibble(station = swept$station_id, value = level, .pred = predict(fitted, swept)$.pred) }) |> list_rbind() } ice <- list(depth_m = sweep(forest, "depth_m"), temperature_c = sweep(forest, "temperature_c")) # the partial dependence is the average over the stations partial <- map(ice, \(d) summarise(d, .pred = mean(.pred), .by = value)) # one slice, as in Linearity and nonlinearity typical <- train |> summarise(across(c(depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3, salinity_psu), \(x) median(x, na.rm = TRUE))) |> mutate(substrate = factor("sand", levels = levels(train$substrate)), season = factor("summer", levels = levels(train$season))) slices <- map(names(partial), \(input) { grid <- tibble(!!input := partial[[input]]$value) rows <- typical |> select(-all_of(input)) |> cross_join(grid) tibble(value = grid[[1]], .pred = predict(forest, rows)$.pred) }) |> set_names(names(partial)) peak_of <- \(d) d$value[which.max(d$.pred)] tibble(Peak = c("Depth (m)", "Temperature (°C)"), `Partial dependence` = map_dbl(partial, peak_of), `One slice` = map_dbl(slices, peak_of)) |> mutate(across(-Peak, \(x) round(x, 1))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Peak | Partial dependence| One slice| |:----------------|------------------:|---------:| |Depth (m) | 24.5| 47.8| |Temperature (°C) | 7.7| 7.2|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} # every training station's prediction with one input set to each of 40 # values over the middle 90% of its range def sweep(fitted, column, kind="average"): result = partial_dependence( fitted, train[fitted.feature_names_in_], [column], kind=kind, percentiles=(0.05, 0.95), grid_resolution=40) return result["grid_values"][0], result[kind][0] # one slice, as in Linearity and nonlinearity typical = train[numeric].median() def one_slice(column, grid): rows = pd.DataFrame({c: [typical[c]] * len(grid) for c in numeric}) rows[column] = grid rows["substrate"], rows["season"] = "sand", "summer" return forest.predict(rows[numeric + categorical]) peaks = {} for column in ["depth_m", "temperature_c"]: grid, average = sweep(forest, column) peaks[column] = { "Partial dependence": grid[average.argmax()], "One slice": grid[one_slice(column, grid).argmax()]} (pd.DataFrame(peaks).T .set_axis(["Depth (m)", "Temperature (°C)"]) .rename_axis("Peak") .round(1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | Peak | Partial dependence | One slice | |:-----------------|---------------------:|------------:| | Depth (m) | 37.4 | 37.4 | | Temperature (°C) | 7.8 | 8 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the curves R/make-example-data.R used, on the log scale true_curve <- list( depth_m = \(depth) -0.55 * ((depth - 80) / 60)^2, temperature_c = \(temperature) -0.60 * ((temperature - 9) / 3)^2 ) shapes <- map(names(partial), \(input) { bind_rows( partial[[input]] |> mutate(curve = "Partial dependence"), slices[[input]] |> mutate(curve = "One slice"), partial[[input]] |> mutate(curve = "Simulation", .pred = exp(true_curve[[input]](value))) ) |> mutate(input, relative = .pred / max(.pred), .by = curve) }) |> list_rbind() shape_plot <- function(which, x_label) { ggplot(filter(shapes, input == which), aes(value, relative, colour = curve, linetype = curve)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("Partial dependence" = ml_palette[["blue"]], "One slice" = ml_palette[["orange"]], Simulation = ml_palette[["grey"]])) + scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Partial dependence" = "solid", "One slice" = "solid", Simulation = "dashed")) + labs(x = x_label, y = "Prediction relative to its peak", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) } shape_plot("depth_m", "Depth (m)") + shape_plot("temperature_c", "Temperature (°C)") + plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The random forest's partial dependence and its one slice against the curves the simulation used (dashed), each divided by its own peak, over the middle 90% of each input's values. Both of the forest's curves find the temperature hump. Neither finds the depth peak: the slice is level from the shallowest depth drawn to about 80 m and then falls, and the partial dependence falls from the start.](partial-effects_files/figure-html/fig-partial-1.png){#fig-partial fig-alt='Two panels, each with a partial dependence curve, a one-slice curve and a dashed simulation curve, scaled so each peaks at 1. Left, depth: the simulation\'s curve is an arch peaking at 80 metres; the partial dependence is highest at the shallowest depth and falls in steps to about 0.57; the slice stays between about 0.93 and 1 to about 80 metres, then falls in steps to about 0.53. Right, temperature: the simulation\'s curve is an arch peaking at 9 degrees; both forest curves sit near 0.5 below 5.5 degrees, rise steeply between 6 and 7 degrees to a peak between 7 and 8 degrees and stay near 0.9 to about 10 degrees; above that the slice falls to about a quarter of its peak and the partial dependence to about 0.58.' width=1600} ::: ::: On temperature the partial dependence peaks at 7.7 °C and the slice at 7.2 °C, both a little cooler than the simulation's 9 °C. They part in the warmest water: there the slice falls to 24% of its peak and the partial dependence only to 58%. The slice answers for one summer station on sand; the average answers for the stations as they are, and the ICE curves below show how much they differ. On depth neither curve has the simulation's arch. The partial dependence is highest at 24 m, the shallowest value drawn, and at the simulation's peak of 80 m it has fallen to 70% of its peak. The slice is level through the shallow half and falls beyond it. So the wrong depth curve does not come from the typical values the slice was held at; it is what the forest learned. ### ICE curves show the temperature hump at nearly every station The same sweep, before averaging, gives one curve for each of the 598 training stations. @fig-ice draws them for temperature. For each station, the table below measures the rise from the coldest temperature drawn to the partial dependence's peak, and the fall from there to the warmest. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # each station's rise from the coldest value drawn to the partial # dependence's peak, and its fall from there to the warmest top <- peak_of(partial$temperature_c) changes <- ice$temperature_c |> summarise(rise = .pred[value == top] - first(.pred), fall = .pred[value == top] - last(.pred), .by = station) changes |> pivot_longer(c(rise, fall), names_to = "change", values_to = "size") |> summarise(`Above zero` = percent(mean(size > 0)), Lowest = round(min(size), 1), Median = round(median(size), 1), Highest = round(max(size), 1), .by = change) |> mutate(change = str_to_sentence(change)) |> rename(Change = change) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Change |Above zero | Lowest| Median| Highest| |:------|:----------|------:|------:|-------:| |Rise |100% | 0.0| 2.6| 8.9| |Fall |98% | -0.7| 2.3| 8.3|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} grid, curves = sweep(forest, "temperature_c", kind="individual") # each station's rise from the coldest value drawn to the partial # dependence's peak, and its fall from there to the warmest top = curves.mean(axis=0).argmax() changes = pd.DataFrame({"rise": curves[:, top] - curves[:, 0], "fall": curves[:, top] - curves[:, -1]}) (pd.DataFrame({"Above zero": (changes > 0).mean().map("{:.0%}".format), "Lowest": changes.min().round(1), "Median": changes.median().round(1), "Highest": changes.max().round(1)}) .set_axis(["Rise", "Fall"]) .rename_axis("Change")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | Change | Above zero | Lowest | Median | Highest | |:---------|:-------------|---------:|---------:|----------:| | Rise | 100% | 0.6 | 1.9 | 4.2 | | Fall | 100% | 0.3 | 1.8 | 4.4 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(ice$temperature_c, aes(value, .pred)) + geom_line(aes(group = station), colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], alpha = 0.25, linewidth = 0.3) + geom_line(data = partial$temperature_c, colour = ml_palette[["blue"]], linewidth = 1.4) + labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Predicted count (individuals)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![ICE curves for temperature: the random forest's prediction for each training station as its temperature is moved and the rest of the station stays as recorded, with their average, the partial dependence, in blue. Almost every curve rises between 6 and 7 °C, stays high to about 10 °C and then falls; the curves differ mostly in height.](partial-effects_files/figure-html/fig-ice-1.png){#fig-ice fig-alt='Several hundred thin grey curves against temperature from about 4 to 13.5 degrees, most between 1 and 10 predicted individuals, a few reaching 17 to 25. Nearly all are level below about 5.5 degrees, rise between 6 and 7 degrees, stay high with small wiggles to about 10.4 degrees, then drop and level off towards the warm end. Higher curves rise and fall by more. A thick blue curve, their average, runs through the lower middle of the bundle with the same shape, from about 3 up to nearly 6 and back to about 3.4.' width=1400} ::: ::: The curve rises from the coldest water to the partial dependence's peak on all but 1 of the 598 stations, and falls again towards the warmest on all but 14 of the 598 stations. The size of the rise differs far more: half the stations rise by less than 2.6 individuals, the largest by 8.9. Stations where the forest predicts many animals anyway gain most from the right temperature, so the curves share a shape and differ in scale. The partial dependence shows where the hump lies; how large it is depends on the station. ### Position as an input leaves the depth curve falling Why is the depth curve wrong? The shelf deepens offshore, so depth follows position, and the forest can give depth an effect that belongs to something about position that no input measures. Position would then be a [confounder](../01-introduction/prediction-and-explanation.qmd#depth-confounds-the-salinity-slope). A second forest is given longitude and latitude as well, and both are scored on the test sites. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} forest_place <- forest_on(c(inputs, "longitude", "latitude")) test_rmse <- \(fitted) rmse_vec(test$abundance, predict(fitted, test)$.pred) place_depth <- sweep(forest_place, "depth_m") |> summarise(.pred = mean(.pred), .by = value) tibble(Model = c("Six inputs", "Six inputs and position"), `Test RMSE` = round(c(test_rmse(forest), test_rmse(forest_place)), 2), `Depth curve's peak (m)` = round(c(peak_of(partial$depth_m), peak_of(place_depth)), 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Model | Test RMSE| Depth curve's peak (m)| |:-----------------------|---------:|----------------------:| |Six inputs | 3.96| 24.5| |Six inputs and position | 3.71| 24.5|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} place = ["longitude", "latitude"] forest_place = forest_on(numeric + place) def test_rmse(fitted): return root_mean_squared_error( test["abundance"], fitted.predict(test[fitted.feature_names_in_])) grid, place_depth = sweep(forest_place, "depth_m") pd.DataFrame({ "Model": ["Six inputs", "Six inputs and position"], "Test RMSE": [test_rmse(forest), test_rmse(forest_place)], "Depth curve's peak (m)": [peaks["depth_m"]["Partial dependence"], grid[place_depth.argmax()]], }).round({"Test RMSE": 2, "Depth curve's peak (m)": 1}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | Model | Test RMSE | Depth curve's peak (m) | |:------------------------|------------:|-------------------------:| | Six inputs | 4.74 | 37.4 | | Six inputs and position | 4.7 | 37.4 | ::: ::: ::: Position helps the predictions: the test RMSE falls from 3.96 to 3.71 individuals. The depth curve keeps its shape. Its peak is still at 24 m, and at 80 m it stands at 83% of that peak, against 70% without position. Position predicts depth closely. A linear regression on longitude and latitude, fitted to the training sites, predicts the depth of the test stations: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} depth_from_place <- linear_reg() |> fit(depth_m ~ longitude + latitude, data = train) augment(depth_from_place, test) |> rmse(depth_m, .pred) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|.metric |.estimator | .estimate| |:-------|:----------|---------:| |rmse |standard | 19.45774|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} depth_from_place = LinearRegression().fit(train[place], train["depth_m"]) root_mean_squared_error(test["depth_m"], depth_from_place.predict(test[place])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> 17.06514082814744 ``` ::: ::: ::: Its RMSE is 19 m: once the place is known, depth is known to within about that. The survey holds few stations that differ in depth but not in place, and no model can tell from these data which of the two the catch follows. The forest is free to give the effect to either, and the curve shows what it chose. ## Partial effects describe the model, and the data decide how far they describe the species A partial dependence plot and its ICE curves are a faithful picture of what a model predicts. On the survey they found the temperature hump at nearly every station, and they showed that the depth curve is not the species' response. Reading a curve as the species' response needs data in which the input varies on its own, for depth, stations at different depths in the same area. [Black boxes and interpretable models](black-box-or-not.qmd) compares the forest with models whose curves can be read directly. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - A **partial dependence plot** sets one input to each value in turn in every row, predicts, and averages. It works for any model and does not depend on where the other inputs are held. - **ICE curves** are the same sweep for each row before averaging. Curves that share a shape show the average describes them; curves that peak in different places show an interaction. - Draw the curves where the data are: a sweep pairs each value with every row's other inputs, including combinations the survey never had. - On the survey the forest's temperature curves rose and fell at nearly every station, by amounts that differed from station to station. - The depth curve stayed highest in shallow water, even with position as an input. Depth follows position on the survey, and no curve can separate what the data do not. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Draw the partial dependence of `substrate`: set every training station to each level in turn and average the predictions. Which level does the forest predict most animals on? 2. Leave `temperature_c` out of the inputs, refit the forest and redraw the depth curve. Does depth take over part of the temperature hump?
